query: Investigate the synthesis of a Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co multi-principal element alloy via high-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering. The starting material is a ball-milled powder exhibiting a body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution. The processing challenge is that magnesium volatility limits the maximum sintering temperature to 1000 °C, while insufficient driving force below 800 °C prevents bulk formation. Existing literature indicates that differences in atomic properties often lead to stable intermetallics and that oxygen intake during milling is a persistent risk. The specific gap is the kinetic mechanism by which high-temperature sintering promotes a specific microstructural evolution that simultaneously enhances hardness, density, and barrier formation for oxidation/corrosion resistance. Request a hypothesis detailing the interplay between sintering temperature, diffusion activity, and the precipitation of secondary phases that act as diffusion barriers. Provide the boundary condition where this mechanism fails (e.g., excessive temperature causing composition deviation), and a falsification experiment involving post-mortem analysis of the passive film structure and oxidation kinetics to distinguish between a diffusion-controlled mechanism and a surface-reaction-limited one.

generation.hypothesis: In Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co multi-principal element alloys processed via high-energy ball milling and spark plasma sintering (SPS), a specific sintering temperature window (850–950 °C) promotes the diffusion-driven precipitation of fine, coherent TiO2 and Al2O3 secondary phases at BCC grain boundaries. These oxides, formed from oxygen intake during milling, act as kinetic diffusion barriers that suppress Mg volatility and grain coarsening, thereby simultaneously enhancing hardness, density, and oxidation resistance. This mechanism fails if the sintering temperature exceeds 980 °C, where the driving force for Mg evaporation and oxide decomposition overcomes the barrier effect, leading to composition deviation and porosity.
generation.material_initial_state: Ball-milled Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co powder exhibiting a body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with nanocrystalline grain size and entrained oxygen impurities.
generation.intervention: Spark plasma sintering (SPS) at a controlled temperature of 850–950 °C for a short dwell time (e.g., 5–10 minutes) to activate diffusion without triggering bulk Mg loss.
generation.conditions: Vacuum or inert atmosphere sintering to minimize external oxygen uptake, with a maximum temperature limit of 1000 °C to prevent Mg volatility.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanometric TiO2 and Al2O3 precipitates forming at BCC grain boundaries, acting as diffusion barriers for Mg and other volatile species.
generation.mechanism: High-temperature sintering activates atomic diffusion, causing the segregation of oxygen and refractory elements (Ti, Al) to grain boundaries. These elements react to form stable oxide precipitates that pin grain boundaries and block the diffusion pathways for Mg, preventing its evaporation and promoting densification. The precipitates also serve as a pre-formed barrier layer against external oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A bulk alloy with >98% theoretical density, significantly increased Vickers hardness (due to precipitation strengthening), and a dense, adherent passive oxide layer that reduces oxidation kinetics by an order of magnitude compared to samples sintered below 800 °C or above 980 °C.
generation.baseline: Samples sintered below 800 °C (insufficient diffusion, low density, no barrier formation) and samples sintered above 980 °C (Mg loss, grain coarsening, porosity, and degraded mechanical properties).
generation.boundary: The mechanism fails when the sintering temperature exceeds 980 °C, where the thermodynamic driving force for Mg volatility and the decomposition of metastable oxides dominate, leading to composition deviation and loss of barrier integrity.
generation.uncertainty: The exact stoichiometry and phase stability of the oxide precipitates (TiO2 vs. Al2O3 vs. mixed oxides) in the presence of Mg are not fully characterized in the provided evidence, and the specific kinetic threshold for Mg evaporation in this specific multi-component system is estimated based on general refractory HEA behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co samples sintered at 800 °C, 900 °C, and 1000 °C. Perform post-mortem analysis using Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) to identify grain boundary precipitates and Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (SIMS) to map Mg distribution. Conduct isothermal oxidation tests at 800 °C and measure the oxide weight gain over time.
measurements: Mg concentration profile across grain boundaries (SIMS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if: (1) No oxide precipitates are observed at the grain boundaries in the 900 °C sample, (2) Mg concentration does not show depletion at the surface or enrichment at grain boundaries in the 900 °C sample compared to 800 °C, or (3) The oxidation kinetics of the 900 °C sample are not significantly slower than the 800 °C sample, indicating the absence of a diffusion barrier mechanism.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Abstract High entropy alloy nanoparticles bring hope to developing more efficient nanomaterials for high‐temperature applications. Nevertheless, the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation about the impact of thermodynamic contributions on their structural properties and remains to be proven. Here, in situ aberration‐corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles (NPs) from 298 to 973 K. Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature. This phase separation that appears progressively with temperature is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems. Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm
